note: MS-H: the gate-law width curve, three points at a matched ~50M-token anchor. d=128 read off the 40h run at its nearest eval (49.6M); d=256 and d=512 are dedicated 50M runs on the identical recipe (B=8, K=64, lr 3e-3, seed 42, q=0.75, window 500, no index) with ONLY the width changed.
headline: The two-point trend does NOT extend. improvement_ratio goes 0.9729 -> 0.9953 -> 0.9777: a maximum at d=256, not a monotone rise.
confound_found: The d=512 arm gated at 19.8% where d=128 and d=256 both gated at 24.7% — stable from the start of the run, not a drift. A3 therefore received ~20% fewer gradient tokens at d=512, so the three ratios are NOT equally dosed and the drop is not attributable to width alone.
what_survives: Per gradient token spent, d=512 is the BEST of the three (0.3547 vs 0.2969 / 0.2937 improvement per M grad-token). Selection did not get worse with width — it got cheaper. The ratio fell because the dose fell.
also: A2 (full gradient) degrades with width at this fixed token budget (4.9161 -> 5.0363 -> 5.0898), as expected: wider models need more tokens. The anchor measures selection efficiency, not model quality.
open: Why the gate fires less often at d=512 is unexplained and is now the load-bearing question — the quantile gate (q=0.75, window 500) is width-agnostic by construction, so a stable 19.8% instead of 24.7% means the SURPRISE DISTRIBUTION itself changed shape with width. That is a finding about the signal, not about the gate.
